concepts.title: Time Complexity
concepts.overview: Time complexity quantifies the amount of computational time an algorithm takes to run as a function of the input size (n). It describes algorithm efficiency and scaling behavior rather than wall-clock seconds.
concepts.whyUse: Critical for predicting how algorithms perform with massive datasets, preventing system bottlenecks, and making informed trade-offs between competing approaches.
howItWorks: Count primitive operations executed by the algorithm as a function f(n).
Identify the dominant term as n approaches infinity.
Drop constant coefficients and lower-order terms to classify into Big-O notation.

example.description: Comparison of linear vs. logarithmic time growth for n = 1,000,000 operations.

operations.name: Constant Time
operations.description: Hash map lookup, array index access

keyTakeaways: Big-O measures worst-case asymptotic upper bounds.
Focus on the dominant order of growth as input size scales.
O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(2ⁿ).

concepts.title: Space Complexity
concepts.overview: Space complexity measures the total amount of memory space required by an algorithm during execution as a function of the input size n, including both input space and auxiliary memory.
concepts.whyUse: Crucial for memory-constrained environments like mobile devices, embedded systems, and distributed stream processors handling massive real-time streams.
howItWorks: Account for fixed memory needed for basic constants and simple variables.
Account for variable dynamic memory allocated on the heap (arrays, graphs).
Account for call-stack frames allocated during nested recursive invocations.

example.description: Call stack frames generated during recursive factorial evaluation of n = 4.

operations.description: Modifies data structures with zero extra allocation

operations.name: Call Stack Overhead
operations.description: Depth d of the recursive call tree

operations.name: Buffer Allocation
operations.description: Auxiliary hash sets, arrays, or queues

pseudocode: // In-place pointer swap: O(1) auxiliary space
keyTakeaways: Auxiliary space refers to temporary memory beyond the input itself.
Recursive solutions always consume stack memory equal to tree depth.
Often traded off against time complexity (e.g. memoization tables).

concepts.title: Recursion
concepts.overview: A computational method where a function solves a problem by calling copies of itself with smaller subproblems until reaching a base termination condition.
concepts.whyUse: Simplifies problem expressions for naturally hierarchical structures like trees, graphs, directory traversal, and divide-and-conquer algorithms.
howItWorks: Define one or more base cases that terminate recursion without further calls.
Deconstruct the problem into smaller subproblems with identical structure.
Combine subproblem results as stack frames unwind toward the root call.

example.description: Calculating factorial(4) = 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 24 via recursive unwinding.

operations.name: Recursive Call
operations.description: Pushes new execution frame to call stack

operations.name: Frame Return
operations.description: Pops active frame and returns computed value

keyTakeaways: Every recursive function requires a guaranteed base case to avoid stack overflow.
Each recursive call pushes arguments and local variables onto the call stack.
Tail-call optimization can convert qualifying recursion into iteration.

concepts.title: Arrays
concepts.overview: A fundamental linear data structure consisting of elements stored in contiguous memory locations, each addressable via a 0-based integer index.
concepts.whyUse: Optimal choice when fast O(1) random access is needed and collection size is known or grows sequentially.
howItWorks: Allocates a contiguous block of memory bytes.
Computes memory addresses directly: Address = BaseAddress + (Index × ElementSize).
Provides instant direct indexing without pointer traversal.

example.description: Sequential contiguous memory allocation with 0-based indices.

keyTakeaways: Contiguous memory layout enables cache-friendly spatial locality.
Instant O(1) random access by index calculation.
Inserting or deleting elements in the middle requires shifting O(n) elements.

concepts.title: Strings
concepts.overview: A sequenced collection of characters represented using encoding schemes such as ASCII or UTF-8, typically implemented as character arrays.
concepts.whyUse: Essential for text processing, tokenization, serialization, pattern recognition, and user communication.
howItWorks: Stores characters sequentially in memory as contiguous byte sequences.
In many languages (Java, Python, JS), strings are immutable; mutations allocate new strings.
Operations often use two-pointer or rolling-hash paradigms.

example.description: Character sequence layout for string 'ALGO'.

operations.name: Substring Extraction
operations.description: Copies k characters to fresh string

keyTakeaways: Immutable strings require StringBuilder or array buffers for efficient concatenation.
String matching algorithms (KMP, Rabin-Karp) reduce search from O(n×m) to linear O(n+m).

concepts.title: 2D Arrays
concepts.overview: A grid-like data structure organized into rows and columns, mapped to 1D memory using row-major or column-major layout.
concepts.whyUse: Used for tabular datasets, matrix computations, dynamic programming memo tables, image pixels, and graph adjacency representations.
howItWorks: Organizes elements with coordinate pairs `[row][col]`.
Row-major mapping computes address: `Base + (row * cols + col) * size`.
Allows efficient nested traversal across rows and columns.

example.description: Matrix indices for a 2x3 grid.

operations.name: Matrix Traversal
operations.description: Visits all R rows and C columns

keyTakeaways: Traversing row-by-row maximizes CPU cache hit rates in row-major environments.

concepts.title: Prefix Sum
concepts.overview: A precomputation technique that builds an auxiliary array where each index stores the cumulative sum of all elements up to that point.
concepts.whyUse: Enables range sum queries on an array in O(1) time after a single O(n) preprocessing step.
howItWorks: Construct prefix[i] = prefix[i - 1] + arr[i].
Calculate range sum between indices L and R: sum(L...R) = prefix[R] - prefix[L - 1].

example.description: Prefix sum array for original values [3, 1, 4, 2].

keyTakeaways: Trades O(n) memory to transform repeated O(n) range queries into O(1) lookups.

concepts.title: Sliding Window
concepts.overview: An algorithmic technique that maintains a continuous subsegment (window) over an array or string, expanding and shrinking boundaries dynamically.
concepts.whyUse: Reduces brute-force O(n²) nested loop subsegment problems into optimal linear O(n) single-pass solutions.
howItWorks: Maintain two pointers, left and right, defining window bounds.
Expand right pointer to include elements until window condition is met.
Contract left pointer to shrink window while preserving valid conditions.

example.description: Window of size k = 3 sliding across an array.

complexity.space: O(1) to O(k) for tracking window elements

keyTakeaways: Both left and right pointers advance at most n times, giving guaranteed O(n) runtimes.

concepts.title: Two Pointers
concepts.overview: A pattern utilizing two reference pointers moving through a linear data structure in tandem, either toward each other or in the same direction.
concepts.whyUse: Solves searching pairs, partitioning, reversing, and cycle detection with O(1) extra space.
howItWorks: Initialize one pointer at the start and another at the end (converging), or both at start (fast/slow).
Evaluate conditions at pointer locations and advance one or both pointers accordingly.

example.description: Target sum pair search on sorted array [1, 2, 4, 7, 11] for target 9.

keyTakeaways: Frequently requires sorted inputs to guarantee monotonic pointer movement.

concepts.title: Linear Search
concepts.overview: The simplest search algorithm that sequentially checks every element in a list until a match is found or the end is reached.
concepts.whyUse: Applicable to unsorted or unordered collections where no prior ordering guarantees exist.
howItWorks: Start from index 0.
Compare each element against the search key.
Return matched index immediately, or -1 if the array is exhausted.

example.description: Checking each element for key = 7 in [4, 2, 7, 1].

keyTakeaways: Requires no preprocessing or sorting.
Suboptimal for frequent queries on large datasets.

concepts.title: Binary Search
concepts.overview: An efficient divide-and-conquer search algorithm that repeatedly halves the search space of a sorted collection.
concepts.whyUse: Orders of magnitude faster than linear search for large datasets; searches 1 billion elements in ~30 comparisons.
howItWorks: Set left and right pointers to start and end of sorted array.
Compute midpoint: mid = left + (right - left) / 2.
If arr[mid] matches target, return mid. If target is smaller, search left half; otherwise search right half.

example.description: Searching for target 23 in sorted array [4, 8, 12, 16, 23, 42].

pseudocode: else if arr[mid] < target: left = mid + 1
keyTakeaways: Input array MUST be sorted.
Avoid integer overflow by calculating mid as left + (right - left) / 2.

concepts.title: Bubble Sort
concepts.overview: A basic comparison-based sorting algorithm that repeatedly steps through the list, comparing adjacent items and swapping them if they are in wrong order.
concepts.whyUse: Primarily used for educational foundations and detecting already-sorted arrays in O(n) with swap flag.
howItWorks: Pass through array comparing pairs (i, i+1).
Swap out-of-order adjacent pairs so larger elements bubble to the end.
Repeat for n-1 passes.

example.description: First pass bubbling largest element 8 to the end: [5, 1, 4, 8].

keyTakeaways: Stable in-place sorting algorithm.
Impractical for large datasets due to quadratic O(n²) comparisons.

concepts.title: Selection Sort
concepts.overview: An in-place comparison sort that divides the array into sorted and unsorted segments, repeatedly finding the minimum element from the unsorted segment and placing it at the front.
concepts.whyUse: Minimizes memory writes; performs at most O(n) swaps, advantageous when write cycles are expensive.
howItWorks: Find index of minimum element in unsorted subarray.
Swap found minimum with first element of unsorted subarray.
Advance boundary of sorted subarray by one position.

example.description: Selecting minimum 1 and swapping into index 0.

keyTakeaways: Always takes O(n²) time regardless of initial ordering.
Makes at most O(n) swaps.

concepts.title: Insertion Sort
concepts.overview: A simple sorting algorithm that builds the final sorted array one item at a time, inserting each element into its appropriate position among previously sorted elements.
concepts.whyUse: Exceptionally fast on small datasets (n < 20) and nearly-sorted arrays; used as hybrid base case in Timsort.
howItWorks: Iterate from index 1 to n - 1.
Compare current element (key) with predecessors.
Shift greater predecessor elements one position up, then insert key.

example.description: Inserting element 3 into sorted prefix [1, 4, 5].

complexity.time: O(n²) worst, O(n) best for sorted input

keyTakeaways: Adaptive algorithm: runs in O(n) time when array is already sorted.
Stable and in-place.

concepts.title: Merge Sort
concepts.overview: An efficient, stable, divide-and-conquer sorting algorithm that divides the array into halves, recursively sorts them, and merges the sorted halves.
concepts.whyUse: Guarantees deterministic O(n log n) performance even in worst case; ideal for linked lists and external disk sorting.
howItWorks: Divide array into two equal halves until single-element arrays remain.
Recursively sort both halves.
Merge two sorted halves by comparing head elements into an auxiliary array.

example.description: Merging sorted halves [2, 5] and [1, 6] into [1, 2, 5, 6].

complexity.time: O(n log n) in all cases

keyTakeaways: Consistent O(n log n) performance regardless of input distribution.
Requires O(n) extra space for arrays.

concepts.title: Quick Sort
concepts.overview: A widely used divide-and-conquer sorting algorithm that selects a pivot element and partitions the array into values smaller than and greater than the pivot.
concepts.whyUse: Often the fastest general-purpose sort in practice due to exceptional cache locality and in-place partitioning.
howItWorks: Choose a pivot element from array.
Partition elements so smaller values are left and larger are right.
Recursively apply quicksort to left and right subarrays.

example.description: Partitioning around pivot 5: [2, 3, 5, 8, 9].

complexity.time: O(n log n) avg, O(n²) worst

keyTakeaways: Randomized pivot selection avoids O(n²) worst case on sorted arrays.
In-place and cache-friendly.

concepts.title: Singly Linked List
concepts.overview: A linear collection of data nodes where each node contains a value and a pointer reference to the next node in the sequence.
concepts.whyUse: Provides O(1) constant-time insertions and deletions at the head without memory reallocation or element shifting.
howItWorks: Nodes are allocated dynamically on the heap at arbitrary memory locations.
Each node stores `data` and `next` pointer.
Traversed sequentially from `head` until `next == null`.

example.description: Node pointers chaining: [10] -> [20] -> [30] -> null.

operations.name: Insert at Head
operations.description: Point new node to head and update head

keyTakeaways: Dynamic size with no wasted preallocated memory.
No random access: reaching index k requires traversing k pointers.

concepts.title: Doubly Linked List
concepts.overview: A linked list where each node contains references to both its next successor and its previous predecessor node.
concepts.whyUse: Allows bidirectional traversal and O(1) node deletion given a direct pointer to the target node.
howItWorks: Each node maintains `prev`, `data`, and `next` references.
Head's prev and Tail's next point to null.
Removal adjusts both neighbor pointers directly.

example.description: Bidirectional links: null <- [A] <-> [B] <-> [C] -> null.

complexity.space: O(n) with extra prev pointer overhead

keyTakeaways: Foundation for LRU Cache implementations when paired with hash tables.

concepts.title: Circular Linked List
concepts.overview: A linked list variation where the last node points back to the first node, forming an unbroken circular loop.
concepts.whyUse: Useful for round-robin CPU task scheduling, media playlist loops, and multiplayer turn management.
howItWorks: The tail node's `next` pointer refers directly back to `head` instead of null.
Traversal must track start node to detect completed cycle.
keyTakeaways: Eliminates null-pointer checks at boundaries.

concepts.title: Linked List Operations
concepts.overview: Core manipulation algorithms for linked lists including insertion, deletion, cycle detection (Floyd's algorithm), and finding the midpoint.
concepts.whyUse: Essential building blocks for technical interviews and low-level data structures.
howItWorks: Use fast and slow pointer pairs (tortoise and hare).
Fast advances 2 nodes per step while slow advances 1 node.
Intersection indicates cycle presence; end indicates midpoint.

example.description: Midpoint detection using slow (step 1) and fast (step 2) pointers.

pseudocode: while fast != null and fast.next != null:
keyTakeaways: Two pointers enable single-pass operations with O(1) auxiliary memory.

concepts.title: Reverse Linked List
concepts.overview: An in-place algorithm that reverses the direction of all pointer links in a singly linked list.
concepts.whyUse: Fundamental list manipulation pattern used in palindrome checks, big integer math, and reordering.
howItWorks: Track three pointers: `prev` (null), `curr` (head), and `next`.
Store curr.next, reverse link to prev, then advance prev and curr forward.
Repeat until curr is null; prev becomes the new head.

operations.name: Pointer Inversion
operations.description: Inverts link between current and previous

keyTakeaways: Must preserve next pointer reference before overwriting curr.next.

concepts.title: Stack
concepts.overview: A linear data structure following the LIFO (Last-In, First-Out) principle, where elements are inserted and removed exclusively from the top.
concepts.whyUse: Essential for expression evaluation, syntax parsing, undo/redo mechanisms, and backtracking depth-first search.
howItWorks: Push: Places a new element onto the top of the stack.
Pop: Removes and returns the topmost element.
Peek: Inspects the top element without removing it.

example.description: Stack state after pushing 10, 20, 30: Top is 30.

keyTakeaways: Strict LIFO ordering ensures most recent items are processed first.
Forms the operational engine of CPU call stacks.

concepts.title: Queue
concepts.overview: A linear data structure following the FIFO (First-In, First-Out) principle, where elements are enqueued at the rear and dequeued from the front.
concepts.whyUse: Essential for breadth-first graph traversal, printer spools, request queues, and asynchronous messaging pipelines.
howItWorks: Enqueue: Appends a new item to the back (tail) of the queue.
Dequeue: Removes and returns the oldest item from the front (head).
Maintains arrival sequence integrity.

example.description: Queue ordering: Front dequeues first.

keyTakeaways: Guarantees fair First-Come, First-Served order.
Array-based queues require ring buffer logic to prevent memory drift.

concepts.title: Circular Queue
concepts.overview: A fixed-size ring buffer implementation of a queue where the last position connects back to the first position.
concepts.whyUse: Avoids wasting empty slots created at the front of an array during dequeue operations without shifting elements.
howItWorks: Uses modulo arithmetic for pointer advancement: `rear = (rear + 1) % capacity`.
Determines full/empty state by comparing front and rear indices.

example.description: Circular ring wrapping around index boundaries.

keyTakeaways: Maximizes fixed-memory efficiency in audio buffers and network sockets.

concepts.title: Deque
concepts.overview: A Double-Ended Queue that supports constant-time element insertion and deletion at both ends (front and back).
concepts.whyUse: Optimal for sliding window maximum problems, palindrome checkers, and bidirectional history caches.
howItWorks: Provides four core operations: pushFront, pushBack, popFront, popBack.
Implemented using doubly linked lists or dynamic circular arrays.

example.description: Double ended operations at left and right.

keyTakeaways: Generalizes both stack and queue into a single high-performance structure.

concepts.title: Priority Queue
concepts.overview: An abstract data type where each element has an associated priority; elements with highest priority are dequeued before lower priority items.
concepts.whyUse: Core component in Dijkstra's shortest path, Prim's algorithm, Huffman encoding, and OS task scheduling.
howItWorks: Typically implemented using a Binary Heap.
Maintains heap property: parent priority >= children priority.
Extract-Max/Min removes root and restores heap order via sift-down.

example.description: Max Priority Queue: Highest priority served first.

keyTakeaways: Binary heap implementation guarantees logarithmic O(log n) maintenance.

concepts.title: Hashing
concepts.overview: A computational method of mapping arbitrary-sized keys to fixed-size table indices using a deterministic hash function.
concepts.whyUse: Delivers near-instantaneous average O(1) lookups, insertions, and deletions across massive datasets.
howItWorks: Pass key through a hash function: `index = hash(key) % capacity`.
Resolve collisions via Separate Chaining (linked lists) or Open Addressing (probing).
Rehash to larger buckets when load factor threshold (e.g. 0.75) is exceeded.

example.description: Mapping string 'user_42' to table index 3.

complexity.time: O(1) average, O(n) worst case collision

keyTakeaways: A good hash function distributes keys uniformly to avoid clustering.
Worst-case O(n) lookups occur if all keys collide into a single bucket.

concepts.title: Hash Map
concepts.overview: An associative array data structure that stores key-value pairs, using hash codes for constant-time value retrieval.
concepts.whyUse: The workhorse data structure of modern software: caches, symbol tables, database indexes, and fast counting.
howItWorks: Stores entries `{key, value}` in hashed buckets.
Key uniqueness is enforced: inserting an existing key overwrites the previous value.
Provides constant-time `get(key)`, `put(key, value)`, and `remove(key)`.

example.description: Key-value mapping: 'alice' -> 95, 'bob' -> 88.

keyTakeaways: Keys must be hashable and immutable to prevent corrupted bucket lookups.

concepts.title: Hash Set
concepts.overview: A collection that stores unique elements with no duplicates, backed internally by a hash table.
concepts.whyUse: Optimal for deduplication, membership testing, and set operations (union, intersection, difference).
howItWorks: Stores unique keys without associated values (or dummy placeholder value).
Rejects insertions of elements already present in the set.

example.description: Unique set elements: { 5, 12, 42 }.

keyTakeaways: Reduces O(n) nested array containment checks to O(1).

concepts.title: Frequency Counting
concepts.overview: A pattern that tallies element occurrence counts using a hash map to solve anagram, majority element, and subarray problems.
concepts.whyUse: Solves complex counting and distribution problems in a single linear O(n) pass.
howItWorks: Iterate through the collection.
For each element, increment `map[element] = (map[element] || 0) + 1`.

example.description: Character counts for string 'banana': { b:1, a:3, n:2 }.

keyTakeaways: Linear time alternative to O(n log n) sorting for counting problems.

concepts.title: Binary Tree
concepts.overview: A hierarchical tree data structure in which each parent node has at most two children, referred to as the left child and right child.
concepts.whyUse: Models hierarchical data such as file systems, DOM trees, decision trees, and expression trees.
howItWorks: Starts with a root node.
Each node contains data and references: `left` and `right`.
Nodes with zero children are leaf nodes.

example.description: Root 1 with left child 2 and right child 3.

operations.name: Insert Child
operations.description: Attaches node to left or right

complexity.space: O(h) stack where h is height

keyTakeaways: A tree with n nodes has exactly n - 1 edges.
Height h is bounded by log₂(n) for balanced trees and n for degenerate linked trees.

concepts.title: Tree Traversal
concepts.overview: Standardized strategies for visiting every node in a tree: Inorder, Preorder, Postorder (Depth-First), and Level-Order (Breadth-First).
concepts.whyUse: Inorder traversal of BST yields sorted values; postorder is ideal for freeing trees and computing sub-tree sizes.
howItWorks: Inorder: Left -> Root -> Right.
Preorder: Root -> Left -> Right.
Postorder: Left -> Right -> Root.
Level-Order: Explores layer-by-layer using a queue.

example.description: Inorder traversal visits left subtree, root, then right subtree.

complexity.space: O(h) for DFS, O(w) for BFS width

keyTakeaways: DFS uses call stack memory proportional to height.
BFS uses queue memory proportional to maximum tree width.

concepts.title: Binary Search Tree
concepts.overview: A binary tree with the BST property: all left-subtree keys are smaller than root key, and all right-subtree keys are greater.
concepts.whyUse: Enables fast O(log n) lookups, insertions, and deletions while maintaining ordered key sequences.
howItWorks: Searching: Compare search key with root; recurse left if smaller, right if larger.
Insertion: Traverse down until reaching null, then attach new node.
Deletion: Handle 3 cases: leaf node, one child, or two children (replace with inorder successor).

example.description: BST with Root 20: Left child is 10 (< 20), Right child is 30 (> 20).

pseudocode: if node == null or node.val == key: return node
if key < node.val: return search(node.left, key)
keyTakeaways: Self-balancing trees (AVL, Red-Black) prevent O(n) worst-case degradation.

concepts.title: Heap
concepts.overview: A specialized complete binary tree satisfying the heap property: in a max heap, parents are >= children; in a min heap, parents are <= children.
concepts.whyUse: Provides immediate O(1) retrieval of the minimum or maximum element, with O(log n) insertions and extractions.
howItWorks: Compactly stored in a 1D array without explicit pointers.
Parent at index i: children at `2i + 1` and `2i + 2`.
Parent of node i: `(i - 1) / 2`.

example.description: Min-heap array representation: Root 5 is smallest.

operations.name: Pop (Extract)
operations.description: Swap root with last, then sift-down

complexity.time: O(1) peek, O(log n) push/pop, O(n) build

keyTakeaways: Complete binary tree property allows zero pointer overhead representation in arrays.

concepts.title: Graph Representation
concepts.overview: A non-linear structure of vertices (nodes) connected by edges, represented via Adjacency Lists or Adjacency Matrices.
concepts.whyUse: Models networks, social connections, road maps, recommendation engines, and dependency trees.
howItWorks: Adjacency List: Array or map of lists storing neighbor vertices for each node; space-efficient O(V + E).
Adjacency Matrix: 2D boolean array of size V × V; fast O(1) edge lookups but consumes O(V²) space.

example.description: Adjacency list for vertex A connected to B and C.

keyTakeaways: Use adjacency lists for sparse graphs (E << V²).
Use adjacency matrices for dense graphs or fast edge presence checks.

concepts.title: BFS
concepts.overview: Breadth-First Search traverses a graph level-by-level, visiting all immediate neighbors before advancing to subsequent depth tiers.
concepts.whyUse: Guaranteed to find the shortest path in unweighted graphs.
howItWorks: Use a queue and a visited set.
Enqueue start node and mark visited.
While queue is non-empty, dequeue vertex u and enqueue all unvisited neighbors.

example.description: BFS queue processing wave order from source 0.

keyTakeaways: Always finds shortest path in unweighted graphs.
Requires tracking visited nodes to prevent cycles in graphs.

concepts.title: DFS
concepts.overview: Depth-First Search explores as deep as possible along each branch before backtracking, using recursion or an explicit stack.
concepts.whyUse: Ideal for cycle detection, topological sorting, connected components, and solving maze puzzles.
howItWorks: Mark current node as visited.
Recursively visit each unvisited neighbor.
Backtrack when all neighbors are exhausted.

example.description: DFS deep dive: 0 -> 1 -> 3 before backtracking to 2.

keyTakeaways: Call stack depth reaches V in worst-case linear graph paths.

concepts.title: Shortest Path
concepts.overview: Algorithms to find the minimum distance path between nodes in weighted graphs, prominently Dijkstra's and Bellman-Ford.
concepts.whyUse: Powers GPS navigation, network packet routing, airline flight planners, and logistics optimization.
howItWorks: Dijkstra: Greedily explores vertex with smallest known tentative distance using a priority queue.
Relaxes outgoing edges: if `dist[u] + weight(u,v) < dist[v]`, update `dist[v]`.

example.description: Shortest path distances from source S: S -> A (2), S -> B (5).

complexity.time: O((V + E) log V) with min-heap

keyTakeaways: Dijkstra requires non-negative edge weights.
Use Bellman-Ford if negative edge weights exist.

concepts.title: Topological Sort
concepts.overview: A linear ordering of vertices in a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) such that for every directed edge u -> v, vertex u comes before v.
concepts.whyUse: Essential for task dependency scheduling, build systems (Make/Gradle), course prerequisites, and package managers.
howItWorks: Kahn's Algorithm: Compute in-degrees of all vertices.
Add all vertices with in-degree 0 to a queue.
Dequeue vertex, append to sorted order, and decrement in-degrees of neighbors.

example.description: Prerequisite order: [Calc 1] -> [Calc 2] -> [Linear Algebra].

keyTakeaways: Only valid on Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs); detects cycles if result length < V.

concepts.title: Recursion Basics
concepts.overview: The computational methodology of formulating problem solutions in terms of simpler instances of the identical problem.
concepts.whyUse: Simplifies mathematical formulas, tree traversals, and nested structure parsing into clean, readable code.
howItWorks: Base Case: Stops recursion without making further recursive calls.
Recursive Step: Reduces problem instance toward base condition.

example.description: Countdown recursive trace: count(3) -> count(2) -> count(1) -> Boom.

keyTakeaways: Missing base cases result in infinite recursion and StackOverflow errors.

concepts.title: Recursive Call Stack
concepts.overview: The internal runtime memory structure that tracks active execution frames, local variables, and return addresses during recursive calls.
concepts.whyUse: Understanding the call stack is critical for preventing stack overflow, analyzing memory, and converting recursion to iteration.
howItWorks: Every function invocation pushes a new stack frame containing arguments and locals.
Reaching base case stops stack expansion; returning pops frames and delivers return values.

example.description: Active stack frames during sum(3): sum(3) -> sum(2) -> sum(1).

pseudocode: // Max recursion depth is constrained by platform stack limits:
keyTakeaways: Stack memory is limited; excessive recursion depths crash the runtime.

concepts.title: Divide & Conquer
concepts.overview: A paradigm that breaks a problem into smaller independent subproblems, solves them recursively, and combines their solutions.
concepts.whyUse: Dramatically reduces complexity: powers Merge Sort, Quick Sort, Binary Search, and Fast Fourier Transform.
howItWorks: Divide: Split problem into smaller instances.
Conquer: Solve subproblems recursively.
Combine: Merge subproblem solutions to solve original problem.

example.description: Binary divide step splitting array of 8 items into two sets of 4.

keyTakeaways: Master Theorem provides closed-form asymptotic runtime analysis for divide-and-conquer recurrences.

concepts.title: Greedy Approach
concepts.overview: An algorithmic paradigm that makes the locally optimal choice at each step with the intent that these choices lead to a globally optimal solution.
concepts.whyUse: Extremely fast and intuitive; delivers O(n log n) or O(n) solutions where dynamic programming would require O(n²).
howItWorks: Must possess Greedy-Choice Property: global optimum can be reached via local choices.
Must possess Optimal Substructure: optimal solution contains optimal sub-solutions.

example.description: Greedy coin change for 36¢ using coins [25, 10, 1]: 25 + 10 + 1.

complexity.time: Often O(n log n) due to initial sort

keyTakeaways: Greedy does not work for all problems; must be mathematically proven optimal.

concepts.title: Activity Selection
concepts.overview: Classic problem of scheduling the maximum number of mutually non-overlapping activities sharing a common resource.
concepts.whyUse: Standard conference room scheduling, CPU task allocation, and interval scheduling.
howItWorks: Sort activities by their finish times in ascending order.
Always pick the activity that finishes earliest and does not conflict with previously picked activity.

example.description: Selected intervals: [1, 3], [3, 5], [6, 9].

keyTakeaways: Sorting by earliest finish time guarantees maximum room for subsequent activities.

concepts.title: Fractional Knapsack
concepts.overview: A knapsack variant where items can be divided into fractions; goal is to maximize total value within weight capacity W.
concepts.whyUse: Optimizes continuous cargo packing, liquid mixing, and budget bandwidth allocation.
howItWorks: Calculate value-to-weight ratio `v[i] / w[i]` for every item.
Sort items by ratio descending.
Take entire item while capacity remains; take fraction of final item to fill remaining capacity.

example.description: Taking items with highest value-per-kg ratio first.

keyTakeaways: Solvable greedily because items are divisible. 0/1 knapsack requires Dynamic Programming.

concepts.title: DP Introduction
concepts.overview: A problem-solving method that solves complex problems by breaking them down into overlapping subproblems and storing subproblem results to avoid redundant calculations.
concepts.whyUse: Converts exponential O(2ⁿ) brute-force recursive algorithms into polynomial O(n) or O(n²) runtimes.
howItWorks: Requires Overlapping Subproblems: subproblems are computed repeatedly.
Requires Optimal Substructure: optimal solution derived from optimal sub-solutions.
Implemented via Top-Down (Memoization) or Bottom-Up (Tabulation).

example.description: Fibonacci: fib(5) reuses fib(3) and fib(2) without recomputing.

keyTakeaways: Identify the state variables and formulate the recurrence relation.
Remember: 'Careful brute force + remembering answers = Dynamic Programming'.

concepts.title: Memoization
concepts.overview: Top-Down dynamic programming strategy that maintains recursive structure while caching function outputs based on input parameter keys.
concepts.whyUse: Natural translation from recursive formulation; only computes subproblems that are actually needed.
howItWorks: Check cache table before computing.
If key exists, return cached result immediately.
Compute answer recursively, store in cache, and return.

example.description: Memo table caching fib(3) = 2 for subsequent calls.

pseudocode: if n in memo: return memo[n]
keyTakeaways: Preserves intuitive top-down thought process.
Subject to recursion stack limits.

concepts.title: Tabulation
concepts.overview: Bottom-Up dynamic programming that iteratively fills an array or table starting from base cases up to the desired target state.
concepts.whyUse: Eliminates call-stack overhead and allows space optimization (e.g. keeping only the last 2 states).
howItWorks: Initialize table with known base cases.
Use nested loops to iteratively populate subsequent entries according to recurrence relations.

example.description: Filling 1D DP table sequentially from left to right.

keyTakeaways: No recursion stack depth concerns.
Can often reduce memory from O(n) to O(1) by retaining only previous row/cells.

concepts.title: 0/1 Knapsack
concepts.overview: Given items with specific weights and values, determine the maximum value achievable within a knapsack capacity W where each item is either taken (1) or left (0).
concepts.whyUse: Classic resource allocation model for budgets, project selections, and hardware constraints.
howItWorks: State: `dp[i][w]` is max value using first i items with remaining capacity w.
Choice: Either exclude item `dp[i-1][w]` or include item `val[i] + dp[i-1][w - wt[i]]`.
Take the maximum of both choices.

example.description: 2D DP table: rows are items, columns are capacities 0..W.

keyTakeaways: Pseudo-polynomial time depends on capacity numeric magnitude W.
Space can be optimized to a single 1D array by iterating capacities backwards.

concepts.title: Longest Common Subsequence
concepts.overview: Finds the longest subsequence present in both strings in the same relative order (not necessarily contiguous).
concepts.whyUse: Powers file diff tools (git diff), DNA genomic alignment, and plagiarism detection.
howItWorks: If characters match (`s1[i] == s2[j]`), `dp[i][j] = 1 + dp[i-1][j-1]`.
If characters differ, `dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])`.

example.description: LCS of 'ABCDE' and 'ACE' is 'ACE' (length 3).

operations.name: Mismatch Branch
operations.description: Max of left or top cell

keyTakeaways: 2D grid dynamic programming pattern tracking prefix alignments.

concepts.title: Backtracking
concepts.overview: A refined brute-force technique that incrementally builds candidates to solutions and abandons ('backtracks') a candidate as soon as it determines it cannot possibly lead to a valid solution.
concepts.whyUse: Solves constraint satisfaction problems, Sudoku solvers, combinatorial permutations, and puzzle games.
howItWorks: Choose: Make a tentative choice and add to current candidate state.
Explore: Recursively check if this choice leads to a full solution.
Unchoose (Backtrack): Revert choice to restore state before trying next alternative.

example.description: Decision tree pruning when candidate violates constraint.

complexity.time: Exponential O(bᵈ) where b is branching factor

keyTakeaways: Pruning early eliminates vast branches of the decision tree.
Always undo state changes to maintain clean state for sibling branches.

concepts.title: N-Queens
concepts.overview: The classic puzzle of placing N chess queens on an N×N chessboard such that no two queens threaten each other.
concepts.whyUse: The quintessential benchmark for backtracking and constraint satisfaction.
howItWorks: Place queens row by row.
For each column in current row, check if position conflicts with existing queens (column, diagonals).
If safe, place queen and recurse to next row. If no column works, backtrack to previous row.

example.description: 4-Queens safe placement: Q placed at [row 0, col 1].

keyTakeaways: Diagonal indexing trick: `row - col` and `row + col` uniquely identify diagonals in O(1).

concepts.title: Subsets
concepts.overview: Generates the power set (all 2ⁿ subsets) of a given collection of elements.
concepts.whyUse: Used in combinatorial generation, feature selection, and knapsack brute-force baselines.
howItWorks: At each element index, make a binary choice: either include the element or exclude it.
Recurse through all elements to generate leaf states representing subsets.
keyTakeaways: Total number of subsets for n items is exactly 2ⁿ.

concepts.title: Permutations
concepts.overview: Generates all n! possible reorderings of a collection of distinct elements.
concepts.whyUse: Essential for Traveling Salesperson brute force, arrangement puzzles, and cryptarithmetic solvers.
howItWorks: Maintain current permutation and a boolean visited array (or in-place swap).
Pick each unused element, append to permutation, and recurse.
Backtrack by removing element and marking unused.

example.description: Permutations of [1, 2, 3]: 6 total arrangements.

keyTakeaways: Factorial complexity O(n!) grows very rapidly (10! = 3.6 million).
